properties.name: The onboarding skill is written — a newcomer can be told where new work belongs
properties.rationale:
WRITTEN AS A SKILL RATHER THAN A TOOL because the answer is a judgement assembled from six reads, not a computation — which part SHOULD own a new thing is exactly the kind of call `dec:report-dont-judge` says reflow2 reports toward and never makes. A tool would have to pick, and picking is the user's.

THE THREE-WAY DISTINCTION IS STATED AT THE TOP because it is the thing most likely to send someone to the wrong place: where-am-i answers what the system IS, impact-check answers what a change to something EXISTING would break, and this answers where something NEW belongs. The first is often the right thing to run before this one, and the skill says so rather than assuming the reader has.

IT ENDS BY REFUSING TO SURVEY. "Give one recommendation first, then the runner-up and what would make it win" — a newcomer handed five balanced candidates has been given the original problem back with more words attached. That is `req:a-question-arrives-with-a-reading` applied to an answer instead of to a question.

⚠️ THE LINT CAUGHT THREE THINGS AND ALL THREE WERE REAL. Two backticked level values (`component`, `subsystem`) read as unknown tool names and needed the field-term allowlist; a stray directory created by a mis-scoped shell command appeared as two nameless skills; and `dec:idea-does-every-served-skill-get-a-command` requires a command per served skill, so the skill would have shipped reachable only by `get_skill`. None of the three would have been caught by reading the file.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
`getting-started/skills/onboarding/SKILL.md`, served, mirrored, and reachable by the `/where-does-it-go` command. Moves `cap:onboarding` from `planned` to `realized` and delivers `req:onboard-newcomer`, accepted since the eight-requirement batch and unbuilt since — BL-101.

NO CORE CHANGE, exactly as the capability said: it assembles machinery that already existed and had never been pointed at this question. `search_design` on the user's own words, `scan_nodes` with `level` for the right rung, `design_regions` and `granularity_report` to narrow, `propagate_from` for what each candidate would reach, `GOVERNED_BY` plus `alternatives_for` and `recall_resolutions` for what already rules there, `AUTHORED_BY` for who to ask, `claim_report` for who is in it now, and `coverage_report` / `detect_gaps` / `seam_report` for what the design cannot see.

THE REQUIREMENT'S HARDEST CLAUSE IS STEP 5 AND IT IS NON-OPTIONAL: "say honestly which parts of the real system the design does not cover". A confident answer drawn from a design that does not model the relevant part is worse than no answer, because the person receiving it cannot tell the silence was ignorance rather than absence.

⭐ AND THE CLAUSE THAT IS NOT IN THE REQUIREMENT BUT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THE SKILL: give the newcomer a NAME. `AUTHORED_BY` means a ruling can be handed over as "this was Anna's call and here is why" rather than as a wall. A decision with a person attached is one a new hire can ask about.
